extracted.intended_audience: scholars and students of psychology, philosophy, and natural sciences; readers interested in scientific methods for classifying mental phenomena
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and methodological standards for organizing and classifying emotions within psychological science, emphasizing natural-history methods, comparative and developmental evidence, physiology, and analytic grounding rather than superficial externals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt the complete natural-history-method (not merely externals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification should follow the natural-history-method 'in its complete form', not merely grouping by external, conspicuous characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely only on obvious objective/subjective aspects displayed in adults; instead base groups on internal, essential characters revealed by analysis and development. Example given: whales were reclassified with mammals after dissection showed internal affinities despite external resemblance to fish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic basis: seek hidden/internal characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask whether 'certain hidden characteristics, on which the obvious ones depend, are the truly significant ones?' — a true classification requires analysis into these hidden characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dissection, microscopic study, and analysis of underlying mechanisms, not only superficial resemblance. The reviewer argues that without such analysis, groupings by externals will be provisional or wrong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use development/ontogeny as classificatory evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The study of development (embryonic and earlier stages) is often necessary to determine true affinities; 'the study of development as a means to classification' is a fundamental criterion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare structures and functions across developmental stages; where adult structure is ambiguous, earlier stages may reveal true relationships (example: Cirrhipedia misclassified until early forms were found). Apply analogous developmental study to emotions (e.g., infancy → maturity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relate classification to nervous-system structure and function
rubrics_metrics.description: A correct account of the emotions must 'correspond with a correct account of the nervous system' — structure and function must harmonize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include general arrangements, minute structure, and mode of evolution of the nervous system when interpreting emotional functions; consider how organic changes in nervous apparatus underlie emotional differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine multiple sources/bases when classifying emotions
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine 'outward objects, diffusive mode or expression, inward consciousness, resulting conduct and institutions' as bases of discrimination and adopt an arrangement of families/orders of emotion from their combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these four complementary perspectives together rather than any single one alone. The page reproduces Bain's explicit list and recommends incorporating all such indications into classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include bodily manifestations with mental description
rubrics_metrics.description: Conjoin 'the description of the mental phenomena' with 'the physical appearances, in so far as I am able to ascertain them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study corporeal embodiments and outward expressions (diffusive waves, organs roused) as intrinsic parts of emotional states rather than treating them as optional externals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study the mode of diffusion or expression as characteristic
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'mode of diffusion' (the manner in which an emotion spreads and the organs it rouses) is 'thoroughly characteristic of any state of feeling.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe which organs are specially roused, the wave-like diffusion, and the manner of action; though current ignorance may limit precision, diffusion remains a key classificatory feature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use comparative psychology (across species, races, and individual development)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aid classification by studying the evolution of emotions through (1) grades of the animal kingdom, (2) differences between lower and higher human races, and (3) the unfolding from infancy to maturity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare which emotions appear earliest and with lowest organization, how others accompany higher endowments, and how emotions correspond to conditions of life; then compare the three lines of development for general truths about emotional origins and grouping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain emotions' origins via habit, experience, and hereditary modification
rubrics_metrics.description: Emotions may be produced and modified by 'accumulated experiences' and habitual activities; repeated combined states can become organic and incipiently reflexive, forming the 'body of the emotion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate historical/social causes (e.g., social life, discipline, division of labour) and ancestral experiences (e.g., birds acquiring fear of man across generations) as explanatory factors for present emotions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for voluntary/involuntary relations and reflex-action doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: The relations of voluntary and involuntary movements are important and 'are elucidated' by familiarity with the modern doctrine of reflex action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate contemporary physiological doctrines (reflex action) when interpreting emotional movements and their classifications; consider how incipient reflexes contribute to emotional states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid classifying emotions by manifest externals alone (externals are superficial)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classifying emotions by their ordinary conscious aspects and external manifestations is a classification 'of emotions by their externals' and is insufficient because many emotional states will resolve, on analysis, into different elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that introspective 'manifest' qualities (pleasure, pain, love, anger) are useful but superficial; deeper analytic decomposition is required to find true relationships and constituents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain interplay of observation and theory; expect provisional classifications
rubrics_metrics.description: 'True theory is needful as a preliminary to correct observation' and the two must 'advance hand in hand'; classifications based on current data are 'provisional' and will be corrected by further analysis and evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat current groupings as approximate generalizations to direct inquiry; be prepared to revise classifications as new observations, analyses, and theoretical frameworks emerge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use social conduct, institutions, and artistic/moral products as classificatory evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Varieties of human conduct and 'machinery created in subservience to our common susceptibilities' (fine art, moral sense, institutions) reveal families of emotion (e.g., aesthetic or moral emotions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine the social manifestations and institutional outcomes of emotions (laws, philanthropy, art) to help delimit emotional categories and their functions in society.
